title: The new moon
hook: Jewish, Muslim and Buddhist calendars follow the moon; Rabbi Joshua walks to Rabban Gamaliel on his own Yom Kippur, and the Qur'an calls new moons fixed seasons
tomorrow: a king asked the Buddha one favor about the full moon. what?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: my week. One page, everything in its turn, built for a beginner. Now the rule grows past the week, to the month, and the month starts in the sky.

Before calendars lived in phones, someone had to watch the sky. In the days of the Mishnah's rabbis, a new month began when witnesses came to the court and said: we saw the new moon. The Mishnah tells of one month when the rabbis disagreed about the witnesses. Rabbi Joshua thought Rabban Gamaliel had accepted bad testimony, which would move the date of Yom Kippur. So Gamaliel sent him an order: come to me with your staff and your money on the day your own count says is Yom Kippur.
screen: `SOMEONE HAD TO WATCH THE SKY.` → `WE SAW THE NEW MOON.` → `TWO RABBIS, TWO COUNTS.` → `COME WITH YOUR STAFF AND YOUR MONEY.`

segments.voice: Carrying a staff and money would break the holy day as Joshua counted it. He was distressed. Rabbi Akiva pointed him to a verse: "which ye shall proclaim in their seasons." The rabbis read it this way: the holy days are the ones the court proclaims. So Joshua took his staff and his money and walked to Gamaliel on his own Yom Kippur. Gamaliel stood, kissed him on the head, and said: come in peace, my teacher and my disciple. That is the teaching the rabbis drew: in Judaism, holy time isn't only read off the sky. It's set by a community that watches the moon together and agrees to keep the same days. Today the Jewish calendar is calculated in advance, but the new month is still marked as Rosh Chodesh, the head of the month, with its own prayers. Many Muslims still watch for the same thin crescent. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "They ask thee, (O Muhammad), of new moons, say: They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." The Prophet, peace be upon him, told his followers to begin and end the fast of Ramadan by sighting the new moon. That's the shared thing: a month that begins by looking up, together. And the honest difference: the Jewish calendar adds a month in some years to keep its festivals in their seasons, so Passover stays in spring. The Islamic calendar follows the moon alone, so Ramadan travels slowly through the seasons.
screen: `JOSHUA WALKS IN ON HIS OWN YOM KIPPUR.` · `MY TEACHER AND MY DISCIPLE.` · `ROSH CHODESH: THE HEAD OF THE MONTH.` · `NEW MOONS: FIXED SEASONS.` · then, large: `THE NEW MOON.`

segments.voice: Find out when the next new moon falls and put a small mark on that day. On the first evening or two after it, you could look west just after sunset for the thinnest crescent. For now, rest your eyes on the nearest window or wall, and picture that dark sky waiting to be watched.
The new moon: the start of the month in the Jewish and Islamic calendars, once declared on witnesses' word, and still watched for by many.
Something to carry: the new moon, a month that starts when people look up together. See you next time.

howItsDone: Jews mark Rosh Chodesh, the new month, with added prayers in the synagogue; Muslims look for the new crescent to begin and end Ramadan, and communities announce the sighting. Buddhist observance days also follow the moon.
